title: CLO Tips Mini-Class - UV Application Techniques
description: CLO Technical Experts Guide You to a Comprehensive Understanding of UV-Related Knowledge and Its Application Techniques
transcript:
In this video, I will explain the application techniques of UV.  
First, let's talk about what UV is.  
UV refers to the two axes of 2D texture space.  
The U level and vertical V correspond to the x-axis and y-axis in a standard 2D sticker.  
UV represents surface details such as the color pattern on the surface of a 3D model.  
After unfolding and processing, it is presented as a 2D image.  
UV tells the software how to wrap the 2D image onto the surface of the 3D model.  
For example, the Santa Claus model in the picture:  
On the left is the flattened unfolded image of the model surface and the UV image of Santa Claus.  
Details such as color patterns and other surface details will be displayed in the corresponding positions on the 3D model.  
When I open the UV image, I can see that the color pattern corresponds to the 3D model.  
When we finish 3D clothing and want to import it into other 3D software, we need to process the UV image to ensure the surface material texture is correctly imported into other software.  

Next, we open a project file package.  
Open the UV editor from the main menu bar under material UV.  
Since this package consists of 2D flat panels, its UV image shows the various panels of the 3D package.  
We can adjust the position of the panels by moving the slider.  
On the right side of the UV editor is a series of UV tools.  

First, we fill in the UV image.  
Click on Automatic UV Fill.  
A window opens.  
In the window, first look at the UV area.  
Here, the default option is to fill the 0 to 1 area.  
Click Apply.  
All UVs will be displayed in the 0 to 1 area,  
which is the first unit area of the first line of the coordinate axis.  
The selected area can be custom-defined and chosen for filling the coordinate area.  
Here, we can use this option to arrange the UV image of a component separately in another area.  
Select the UV image of the component.  
Set the selected area to 1 to 2.  
Click Apply.  
In this way, the UV image of the component can be filled into the 1 to 2 area.  
Select the UV again.  
In this way, the UV image of the component can be filled in the 0 to 1 area.  
This allows enlarging the accessories and the UV version to a certain extent,  
improving the clarity of the texture.  
Because in most 3D application software, the only usable UV space is the 0 to 1 coordinate space.  
To better integrate with most 3D software, it is recommended to fill the 0 to 1 coordinate area.  
In this case, all UVs need to be filled again into the 0 to 1 area.  

Next, let's talk about the meaning of these options.  
The first is Fill In.  
Through this, the coordinate area of the UV image can be set.  
The value range is 0.001 to 0.999.  
The larger the value, the greater the coordinate space between the panels.  
For example, when I change the value to 0.050, you can see that the coordinate space between the panel UVs becomes larger.  
The corresponding UV image is reduced.  
We will change it back to 0.001.  

Next, look at Accuracy.  
The value can be adjusted between 1 and 5.  
The larger the value, the more accurate the layout placement.  
To ensure the accuracy of the UV layout and a more reasonable use of UV space,  
while also requiring an appropriate calculation speed.  
The default value is 3.  
But when the number of panels is very large and the layout speed slows down,  
the accuracy can be lowered to produce a quicker layout result.  

Next is Fixed Ratio.  
Due to the relative size of the UV panel,  
the default is the same as the 2D panel.  
The size ratio of the current UV image that should be selected can be locked,  
to maintain the ratio consistent with the 2D panel during the filling process.  
Therefore, Fixed Ratio is generally selected.  
If Fixed Ratio is canceled and then filled,  
you can see that to increase the usage rate of UV space,  
some panels will be enlarged or reduced.  
This leads to differences in clarity levels between different panels on the final 3D model.  
Ctrl + Z returns to the previous UV layout state.  
Restore the normal ratio of the panel or right-click in the blank area directly.  
Select all UVs to be rearranged to the position of the 2D panel window.  
This will make the UV and 2D panel layout consistent again.  
Select Fixed Ratio.  

Next is Rotation.  
Select Rotate and then click Apply.  
You can see that to increase the usage rate of the UV space,  
some UV panels are rotated.  
For UV images with patterns such as lines and flowers,  
if you want to keep the pattern consistent in direction,  
do not select Rotate.  
If the pattern direction of individual panels is inconsistent,  
you can right-click the UV of the panel,  
and select to rotate the UV pattern horizontally or vertically to achieve consistency.  

Next is Optimize Layout.  
Optimize Layout is a more advanced calculation method.  
It maximizes the usage rate of UV space,  
to obtain a clearer and higher-quality UV layout,  
and minimize space waste.  
This will make the final pattern as clear as possible.  
In contrast, Optimize Layout takes longer to calculate.  
Here, we choose Optimize Layout.  

One more thing to note:  
The leather fabric used in this bag,  
the back and sides use different materials and colors from the front and sides.  
So how do we show the pattern of the back and sides  
and do the UV layout together?  
First, select the leather fabric pattern used in the application.  
At the bottom of the property editor,  
find UV Expansion.  
Open the back and sides.  
Select the moving side pattern again.  
You can see the UV pattern of the back and sides is displayed.  
If the UV pattern of the back and sides is not displayed,  
you need to check whether the surface with the dense pattern is unfolded.  

Return to the UV Fill window.  
After setting the options in the UV Fill window,  
click Apply.  
The UV pattern layout is completed.  
You can apply the UV quick snapshot below.  
The current UV layout is exported as a 2D image  
as a reference trial.  

Next is Baking Pattern.  
Based on the current UV layout,  
corresponding patterns, line drawings, calligraphy, etc.,  
and different materials are baked and stored together.  
Before that,  
you can check all patterns through the top left corner.  
Open Baking Pattern.  
Set the save path and pixel size.  

Next is Fill Pattern On/Off.  
You can extend the pattern to the UV edge,  
set custom pixels, or unlimited extension,  
to prevent visible gaps in the final pattern as shown in the picture below.  

The baking pattern moves under the UV.  
Select the plate that needs to be moved.  
Click UV Move.  
You can move the plate up/down or left/right.  
Move the entire position.  
At the bottom distance,  
you can enter the unit distance moved per step.  
Here is 1,  
which moves one unit area each time.  
Enter 0.5,  
which moves 0.5 units each time.  
This tool is generally used to adjust the overall position of the UV pattern.  

After processing the UV pattern of the 3D bag,  
move it to another 3D format.  
This process will also export the UV pattern of the file.  
For example, this time I need to move the file to FBX format.  
In the Spring window, I choose Single Target.  
Single Target can merge all plates into a complete grid and export it.  
Multiple Targets will export each plate as a separate grid.  
Then select which to export.  
The thin option outputs only the flat grid.  
The thick option includes the fabric thickness.  
So here I choose the thick one.  

Next, make sure to click on Unified UV Coordinates.  
This way, all UV information of the 3D bag can be combined into a single and orderly UV sticker,  
ensuring that the entire bag’s pattern is correct and even.  
After clicking Unified UV Coordinates, some options appear below.  
Let's look at them separately.  

The first is Picture Size.  
It controls the size of the UV pattern.  
Generally, the input number is 1024.  
The larger the number, the clearer the FBX pattern will be,  
but the corresponding model size will also be larger.  

The second is Fill Pattern.  
The default is 5 pixels.  
What does it do?  
Let's look at the following example.  
In the new Colo program, we import an FBX.  
The fill pattern of this FBX is 0.  
This means the fill pattern does not extend beyond the edge.  
We can see that the edge plus the partition parts appear pixelated.  
This is because the printed version is thick.  
According to the UV concept,  
the fill pattern of the partition extends a certain distance,  
to ensure the part with thickness is fully wrapped with fill pattern.  

Here I set the fill texture to 8.  
This means the edge of the UV image will have an 8-pixel texture fill.  
This ensures the entire model is covered with texture.  

Next, we will import another FBX.  
This FBX is set to 8-pixel texture fill.  
After zooming in, you can see the edge looks normal.  

Note:  
To prevent UVs from overlapping after texture fill,  
it is recommended to slightly enlarge the edge of the UV image during UV arrangement.  
For example, input 0.005 here in Fill,  
so that there will be a little more space between the sheets,  
providing sufficient space for texture fill.  

After setting the texture fill,  
select the type of sticker to save below.  
Click to confirm and export the FBX.  
You can then edit the exported FBX in other 3D software.  

Here we can edit the import.  
Because the exported model UV image is PNG,  
the imported model will have a transparent effect.  
At this time, you need to enable high-quality rendering to check it normally.  
The UV image can be imported into image editing software,  
such as PSAI.  
For example, I made color adjustments to the UV image.  
You can apply the edited UV image to the texture in this column.  
This can make the FBX model more colorful.  

The above is the content of UV application skills.  
Thank you for watching.

chunks.content: ## Introduction to UV Mapping and Its Role in 3D Modeling This section explains the fundamental concept of UV mapping, including the terminology of U and V axes, their relationship to 2D texture space, and how UV coordinates control the application of 2D images onto 3D surfaces. It clarifies how surface details like color patterns are represented and mapped onto 3D models. UV refers to the two axes in 2D texture space: U (horizontal, x-axis) and V (vertical, y-axis). These coordinates correspond to how a 2D image (texture) is wrapped onto a 3D model's surface. After unfolding a 3D model, its surface is flattened into a 2D image called a UV map, which guides software to correctly place texture details on the model. For example, a Santa Claus 3D model's surface is unfolded into a UV image where color patterns correspond exactly to areas on the 3D shape. When creating 3D clothing or assets intended for use across different 3D software, proper UV processing ensures surface textures transfer correctly. --- ## UV Editor and Basic UV Filling Techniques This section covers practical steps to open and manipulate UV layouts using a UV editor, including automatic UV filling, coordinate areas, and repositioning UV islands (panels) within the UV space. Open the UV editor via the main menu under "Material UV." A typical package may consist of multiple 2D flat panels representing different parts of the 3D model. You can adjust the position of these panels using sliders. To fill the UV image automatically: - Click **Automatic UV Fill**. - In the dialog, the default fill area is from 0 to 1 on both U and V axes, corresponding to the primary UV coordinate space. - Click **Apply** to arrange all UVs within this 0 to 1 unit square. You can customize the fill area to other ranges (e.g., 1 to 2) to place components in separate UV spaces for organizational or clarity purposes. However, most 3D software only uses the 0 to 1 UV space, so final textures should be fitted within this area for compatibility. --- ## UV Fill Options and Their Effects This section details the configurable parameters in the UV fill process, explaining their impact on layout accuracy, UV island spacing, scaling, rotation, and overall texture quality. - **Fill In**: Controls spacing between UV panels; values range from 0.001 to 0.999. Larger values increase gaps, reducing panel size. - **Accuracy**: Ranges from 1 to 5. Higher values produce more precise UV layouts but require longer computation. The default is 3. For models with many panels, lowering accuracy can speed up processing. - **Fixed Ratio**: Maintains the original aspect ratio of UV panels consistent with their 2D counterparts. Keeping this enabled prevents distortion and preserves texture clarity. Disabling it allows resizing UV islands to maximize space but can cause inconsistent texture resolution. - **Rotation**: Allows UV panels to be rotated to better utilize UV space.

chunks.content: Higher values produce more precise UV layouts but require longer computation. The default is 3. For models with many panels, lowering accuracy can speed up processing. - **Fixed Ratio**: Maintains the original aspect ratio of UV panels consistent with their 2D counterparts. Keeping this enabled prevents distortion and preserves texture clarity. Disabling it allows resizing UV islands to maximize space but can cause inconsistent texture resolution. - **Rotation**: Allows UV panels to be rotated to better utilize UV space. Useful for increasing packing efficiency but may disrupt directional patterns (e.g., lines or floral designs). If rotation causes pattern inconsistency, individual UVs can be rotated manually horizontally or vertically. - **Optimize Layout**: An advanced algorithm that maximizes UV space usage, producing clearer, higher-quality layouts with minimal wasted space. It takes longer than standard fills but improves final texture quality. --- ## Handling Multi-Material UV Patterns This section explains how to manage UV layouts when different parts of a model use distinct materials or colors, such as leather textures on different bag sections. For example, a bag’s leather fabric on the back and sides uses different materials/colors than the front. To display and layout these patterns together: - Select the leather fabric pattern in the material editor. - In the property editor, locate **UV Expansion**. - Open the back and sides sections to reveal their UV patterns. - If these UV patterns do not display, verify that the surface with the dense pattern is properly unfolded. After configuring, apply the UV fill options and click **Apply** to finalize the UV layout. --- ## Exporting and Snapshotting UV Layouts This section covers exporting UV layouts as 2D images for reference and preparing textures for baking. After completing the UV layout, use the **UV Quick Snapshot** feature to export the current UV as a 2D image. This snapshot serves as a reference for texture painting or further editing outside the 3D software. --- ## Baking Patterns and Texture Extensions This section explains baking textures based on the UV layout and methods to avoid visible seams by extending textures beyond UV edges. - **Baking Pattern**: Combines patterns, line drawings, calligraphy, and different materials according to the UV layout and stores them together. - **Fill Pattern On/Off**: Extends the texture pattern beyond UV edges by a custom pixel value or unlimited extension to prevent gaps visible on the final model. - Textures that do not extend beyond UV edges can cause pixelation or gaps, especially on thick or partitioned materials. --- ## UV Pattern Movement and Fine Adjustments This section discusses precise UV pattern adjustments using the UV Move tool. - Select a UV panel or plate and activate **UV Move**. - Move the panel up/down or left/right by defined unit distances. - The movement step size can be set (e.g., 1 unit or 0.5 unit) for fine control. - This is typically used for adjusting the overall position of UV patterns.

chunks.content: - Textures that do not extend beyond UV edges can cause pixelation or gaps, especially on thick or partitioned materials. --- ## UV Pattern Movement and Fine Adjustments This section discusses precise UV pattern adjustments using the UV Move tool. - Select a UV panel or plate and activate **UV Move**. - Move the panel up/down or left/right by defined unit distances. - The movement step size can be set (e.g., 1 unit or 0.5 unit) for fine control. - This is typically used for adjusting the overall position of UV patterns. --- ## Exporting 3D Models with UVs to FBX Format This section outlines exporting the processed 3D model and UV layout to FBX format for use in other 3D software. - Choose **Single Target** to merge all UV plates into a complete grid during export. - **Multiple Targets** will export each UV plate separately. - Select between **Thin** (flat grid only) and **Thick** (includes fabric thickness). Thick is recommended for accurate material representation. Enable **Unified UV Coordinates** to combine all UV information into a single, orderly UV sticker. This ensures the entire model’s texture pattern is consistent and error-free. --- ## FBX Export Settings: Picture Size and Fill Pattern This section explains key FBX export parameters affecting texture resolution and edge quality. - **Picture Size**: Typically set to 1024. Higher values produce clearer textures but increase file and model size. - **Fill Pattern**: Default is 5 pixels. This extends the texture beyond UV edges to prevent visible seams or pixelation, especially important for thick materials. Example: An FBX with fill pattern set to 0 shows pixelated edges; increasing fill pattern to 8 pixels results in smooth, seamless edges. --- ## Best Practices to Prevent UV Overlap and Texture Issues This section provides recommendations to avoid UV overlapping and texture artifacts during fill and export. - Slightly enlarge UV edges in the UV arrangement phase (e.g., entering 0.005 in the Fill setting) to create buffer space between UV islands. - This buffer prevents overlaps and provides room for texture fills to extend without visible seams. --- ## Editing UV Images and Applying Textures This section describes how to utilize exported UV images for texture editing and reapply them to models. - Exported UV images are typically PNG files with transparency. - Enable high-quality rendering in 3D software to accurately preview textures. - UV images can be edited in image editing software such as Photoshop (PSAI). - After editing (e.g., color adjustments), reapply the modified UV image to the model’s texture slot to enhance appearance and customization. --- ## Summary This document detailed the comprehensive workflow and technical considerations for UV application techniques in 3D modeling, covering UV concepts, editor usage, filling options, multi-material handling, baking, export settings, and texture editing. Proper UV management ensures high-quality, clear textures and compatibility across 3D software platforms.
